title: Romans 8:28: what it promises, and what it does not

line.younger: A verse people say when something sad happens. Seven pictures look closely at what it promises, and at what it does not.
line.older: One of the most quoted verses in the Bible, read in its own chapter: what it does not say, what it does, what the good is, and what the promise rests on.

poster: A man sits writing on a scroll by the light of a small lamp, with the night sky in the window behind him.

frames.name: A verse people reach for
frames.still: A man sits writing on a scroll by the light of a small lamp, with the night sky in the window behind him.
frames.younger: When something sad happens, people often say this verse. It is a true and good promise. But it is easy to get wrong. So look closely at what it says, and at what it does not say.
frames.older: Few verses are quoted more often to people in pain, and few are quoted more carelessly. It is a real promise, written by a man who had been beaten, shipwrecked and jailed. It deserves to be read in its own chapter.

verse.text: And we know that God works all things together for the good of those who love Him, who are called according to His purpose.

frames.name: Not that everything is good
frames.still: After a storm: a house with part of its wall fallen, a bare tree, and a dark cloud moving off. A woman and a child stand looking at it.
frames.younger: The verse does not say that everything that happens is good. Some things are bad, and sad, and wrong. The Bible never asks you to pretend that they are not.
frames.older: The verse does not say that every event is good in itself. The “all things” in this chapter include present sufferings, a groaning creation, and trouble, famine and sword. Paul does not call those things good. He says they cannot defeat God's purpose.

verse.text: Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? Shall trouble or distress or persecution or famine or nakedness or danger or sword?

frames.name: Not that it all works out
frames.still: A person sits alone on the ground beside a tree with no leaves, under a grey sky.
frames.younger: It also does not promise that everything will turn out the way we hoped: that the sickness will go away, or that the sad thing will be undone. Sometimes it is not.
frames.older: Nor does it promise that believers will always see a happy outcome: that the illness will lift, or the loss will be explained. The family catechism says it plainly. The verse does not promise that all things are good, only that God is working in all of them.

frames.name: What it does say
frames.still: A man in a fine robe holds out his hands to three men who kneel before him, with jars and sheaves of grain around them.
frames.younger: Here is what it does say. God is at work in all things, even the worst things, for the good of his people. Long before Paul, Joseph said the same to the brothers who had sold him: you meant it for evil, but God meant it for good.
frames.older: What it says is both more modest and more solid: God works all things together for the good of those who love him. The subject of the sentence is God. Evil stays evil, and God is at work in it, as Joseph told the brothers who had sold him.

verse.text: what you intended against me for evil, God intended for good

frames.name: What the good is
frames.still: Jesus walks ahead along a road, and a man and a child walk behind him in his steps.
frames.younger: And what is the good that God is working toward? The next verse tells us. It is not that we get rich or stay comfortable. It is that we become like Jesus.
frames.older: The good is defined in the next verse, and it is more than comfort or success: to be conformed to the image of his Son. Christians read that verse's words about foreknowing and predestining differently. They agree that this is a promise of God's faithfulness to his people in suffering.

verse.text: to be conformed to the image of His Son

frames.name: Room to groan
frames.still: Night. A person kneels bowed to the ground under a tree, and above them, among lines of wind, is one small gold flame.
frames.younger: This chapter does not tell sad people to cheer up. It says the whole world is groaning, and we groan too. And God's own Spirit helps us, and prays for us when we have no words.
frames.older: The chapter that holds this promise is full of groaning: creation groans, believers groan, and the Spirit himself intercedes. The verse is not a way to hurry anyone past grief. It was written from inside it.

verse.text: the Spirit helps us in our weakness.

frames.name: Nothing can separate
frames.still: Morning. A family stands close together on a road, looking toward a hill where an empty cross stands in the rising sun.
frames.younger: The chapter ends with the surest thing of all. Nothing, not sadness, not danger, not even death, can separate God's children from his love. That is the promise underneath the promise.
frames.older: The chapter ends with what the promise rests on. God did not spare his own Son. So nothing in all creation can separate his people from his love. That is the ground this verse stands on.

verse.text: nor anything else in all creation, will be able to separate us from the love of God that is in Christ Jesus our Lord.

think.younger: What is the difference between saying everything is good and saying God is working in everything?
think.older: Has this verse ever been quoted to you too quickly? What would it have sounded like if the person had read you the whole chapter?

care: If something hard is happening to you or to someone you love, you do not have to carry it alone. Talk with a parent, a pastor or another adult you trust, or look at Find Help.

differ.text: Christians read the words about God foreknowing and predestining in the next verse differently: Reformed readers as God's prior choosing love, Arminian readers as God's foreknowledge of those who would believe. Both agree that the verse is a promise of God's faithfulness to his people in suffering, and not a denial that suffering is real or evil. This moving picture takes no side.
